shape.subject: Mathematics
shape.scope: Numbers and their operations (primes, HCF/LCM, squares/cubes/roots, standard form, estimation, significant figures); ratio and proportion (incl. map scales, direct and inverse proportion); percentage (incl. reverse percentage); rate and speed (incl. average speed, conversion of units); financial mathematics (simple and compound interest, hire purchase, money exchange, taxation, utilities bills); algebraic expressions and formulae (expansion, factorisation incl. grouping and quadratic trinomials, algebraic fractions, changing the subject, algebraic identities); functions and graphs (linear, quadratic incl. completed-square and factorised forms, cubic, reciprocal y=a/x and a/x^2, exponential y=ka^x, drawing on a grid from a table of values, gradient of a curve by a tangent, solving equations by drawing a suitable line); equations and inequalities (linear, simultaneous linear, quadratic by factorisation / completing the square / the formula, fractional equations reducing to quadratics, linear inequalities incl. double inequalities, word problems leading to these); set language and notation (union, intersection, complement, subsets, Venn diagrams with numbers of elements); matrices (display of information, addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication of two matrices, interpretation of the product; no inverses); problems in real-world contexts (reading tables and information sheets, making and justifying a decision, estimating a cost or a quantity); angles, triangles and polygons (angle properties of parallel lines, triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons; construction with ruler, compasses and protractor: perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors; scale drawings); congruence and similarity (tests, ratios of lengths, areas and volumes of similar figures and solids); properties of circles (symmetry properties: equal chords, perpendicular from centre, tangents from a point; angle properties: angle at centre, angle in a semicircle, angles in the same segment, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, tangent-radius; reasons stated); Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry (sine, cosine and tangent for acute and obtuse angles, sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle as ½ab sin C, bearings, angles of elevation and depression, simple 3-D problems); mensuration (area of a triangle, parallelogram, trapezium, circle; arc length and sector area with the angle in RADIANS or degrees; surface area and volume of a prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone and sphere; composite solids); coordinate geometry (gradient, length, midpoint is NOT required, equation of a straight line y=mx+c, parallel lines, area of a rectilinear figure by shoelace is NOT required — use base×height or split into triangles); vectors in two dimensions (column vectors, magnitude, position vectors, addition, scalar multiples, collinearity, expressing one vector in terms of others, ratios of areas of triangles with a common height or on the same base); data handling and analysis (tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, line graphs, histograms with equal class widths, dot diagrams, stem-and-leaf, box-and-whisker plots, cumulative frequency curves, median, quartiles, percentiles, range, interquartile range, mean and standard deviation for grouped and ungrouped data, comparing two distributions in context); probability (single events, combined events by possibility diagrams and tree diagrams, with and without replacement, mutually exclusive and independent events). NOT in 4052: calculus, logarithms, surds, the binomial theorem, trigonometric identities, the R-formula, quadratic inequalities, matrices inverses and determinants, vectors in three dimensions, the shoelace formula, the midpoint formula.
shape.register:
REGISTER — how SEAB asks (4052)
- Plain, exact, economical English. Instructions are imperatives: Find, Calculate, Work out, Write down, Simplify, Factorise, Expand, Solve, Show that, Explain why, Give a reason, Complete the table, Draw, Describe, Estimate, Express, State.
- Parts are labelled (a), (b), (c), with sub-parts (i), (ii). Every part carries its marks. A 1–3 mark question is often a single unlabelled part.
- A scientific calculator is allowed on BOTH papers. Never write "a calculator must not be used". The paper's rubric already says: non-exact answers to 3 significant figures, angles to 1 decimal place, π = calculator value or 3.142 — so a question states a precision only when it wants something else ("correct to 2 decimal places", "in its simplest form", "in terms of π", "as a fraction in its lowest terms", "in standard form", "to the nearest cent").
- Angles are in DEGREES with the degree sign ($58^\circ$); a sector angle in radians is stated as "1.8 radians". Bearings are three-figure ($048^\circ$). Money is dollars and cents ($\$92.75$).
- Contexts are short, concrete and Singaporean-neutral (a garden fountain, a box of apples, a map of Singapore, a candle business): the situation in one or two sentences, units given, then the parts. Never chatty, never a story.
- "Show that" states its target exactly ("Show that $x^2 - 102x + 1440 = 0$", "Show that $p = 2.5$") and a later part uses it. "Explain why …" / "Give a reason for your answer" / "Is he correct?" parts are worth 1 mark and expect one sentence with a number in it. A circle-properties question says "Give a reason for each step of your working."
- Statistics and probability parts ask for interpretation in context ("By commenting on the means and the standard deviations, compare …", "Explain what this tells you about …").
- Paper 1 (27 short questions, 90 marks): each question tests ONE idea in 1–7 marks, answered in the space provided; the paper walks the syllabus (number, algebra, geometry, statistics interleaved), with the vector and mensuration questions near the end.
- Paper 2 (9 long questions, 90 marks): each question is 8–12 marks in 3–5 parts. Early questions are ALGEBRA MEDLEYS whose parts (a), (b), (c), (d) are separate short problems on different algebra skills. Later ones are one context developed through parts: a graph question (a table of values with two blanks, "On the grid, draw the graph of …", a gradient by a tangent, "By drawing a suitable straight line, solve …"), a trigonometry-on-the-ground question with bearings and a mast, a statistics + probability question over a table or histogram, a circle-properties + circular-measure question, a speed/quadratic question ("Show that … = 0", solve to 2 decimal places, reject a root, interpret), and the last question is a PROBLEM IN A REAL-WORLD CONTEXT: an information sheet (a table of prices, rates or measurements) followed by parts that end in a 5–7 mark "Suggest a suitable … Justify your answer" or "Is it worth …? Show your working" decision.
- Marks follow the work: about 1 mark per 1.5 minutes. 1 mark: read/state/one-line. 2 marks: one routine. 3–4 marks: a short chain. 5–7 marks: a multi-step argument or a decision with working.

title: E Math · Set 3 · Paper 2 · O-Level format

question.stem:
In Singapore, a restaurant adds a service charge of $10\%$ to the menu price of the food ordered.
Goods and Services Tax (GST) is then charged on the total of the menu price and the service charge.
On 1 January 2024 the rate of GST increased from $8\%$ to $9\%$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
In February 2024, Mei Ling orders food with a menu price of $\$120$.
Calculate the total amount she pays.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
In March 2024, Raj pays a total of $\$95.92$ for his food.
Calculate the amount of GST he paid.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Members of the restaurant receive a discount of $10\%$ on the menu price.
The service charge and GST are then added to the discounted price.
Kumar is a member. He says that, for him, the discount cancels out the service charge, so he pays only the GST on top of the menu price.
Explain why Kumar is wrong and find the percentage by which the total a member pays exceeds the menu price.
parts.answer: Kumar is wrong because $0.9 \times 1.1 = 0.99$, not $1$: a $10\%$ discount followed by a $10\%$ service charge leaves $99\%$ of the menu price, not $100\%$. A member pays $0.9 \times 1.1 \times 1.09 = 1.0791$ times the menu price, so the total exceeds the menu price by $7.91\%$ (not $9\%$).

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
On 1 January 2024 the restaurant also raised all its menu prices by $5\%$.
Rashid is not a member of the restaurant.
In January 2024, Rashid paid $\$14.19$ more for a set of dishes than he would have paid for the same set of dishes in December 2023.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Calculate the menu price of the set of dishes in December 2023.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: Calculate the total amount Rashid paid in January 2024.

question.answer: (a) $\$143.88$ (b) $\$7.92$ (c) Kumar is wrong ($0.9 \times 1.1 = 0.99$); a member pays $7.91\%$ above the menu price (d)(i) $\$200$ (d)(ii) $\$251.79$
skills: chain two percentage additions in the right order (GST is charged on the menu price plus the service charge, so multipliers 1.1 then 1.09), and recover the GST inside a total by undoing only the last stage (total divided by 1.09, then subtract) rather than taking 9% of the total

explain with multipliers why a 10% discount does not cancel a 10% service charge (0.9 x 1.1 = 0.99, not 1), and chain the third multiplier to find that a member pays 7.91% above the menu price, not 9%

form a linear equation in the December 2023 menu price from the difference between two multiplier chains (5% price rise with 9% GST against the old prices with 8% GST), where the three changes do not add to a single 6%
question.solution:
(a) Service charge: $120 \times 1.1 = 132$.
GST at $9\%$ on $\$132$: $132 \times 1.09 = 143.88$.
**Answer: $\$143.88$**

(b) GST was charged on the amount after the service charge, so that amount is $95.92 \div 1.09 = 88$.
GST paid $= 95.92 - 88 = 7.92$.
**Answer: $\$7.92$**
(Taking $9\%$ of the total gives $0.09 \times 95.92 = \$8.63$, which is wrong: the GST is $9\%$ of $\$88$, not of $\$95.92$.)

(c) Take a menu price of $\$100$ (or let it be $\$x$).
After the member discount: $100 \times 0.9 = 90$.
After the service charge: $90 \times 1.1 = 99$.
So the discount and the service charge do not cancel: $0.9 \times 1.1 = 0.99$, and the member is charged on $\$99$, not $\$100$.
After GST: $99 \times 1.09 = 107.91$.
$107.91 - 100 = 7.91$, so the total exceeds the menu price by $7.91\%$.
**Answer: Kumar is wrong because $0.9 \times 1.1 = 0.99 \neq 1$; a member pays $7.91\%$ more than the menu price, not $9\%$.**

(d)(i) Let the menu price of the set in December 2023 be $\$x$.
December 2023 total (service charge $10\%$, GST $8\%$): $x \times 1.1 \times 1.08 = 1.188x$.
January 2024 menu price: $1.05x$.
January 2024 total (service charge $10\%$, GST $9\%$): $1.05x \times 1.1 \times 1.09 = 1.25895x$.
$1.25895x - 1.188x = 14.19$
$0.07095x = 14.19$
$x = 200$
**Answer: $\$200$**
(Treating the changes as a single rise of $6\%$ gives $0.06x = 14.19$, $x = \$236.50$; forgetting that GST was $8\%$ in December gives $0.05995x = 14.19$, $x = \$236.70$. Both look plausible and both are wrong.)

(d)(ii) January 2024 total $= 1.25895 \times 200 = 251.79$.
(Check: December 2023 total $= 1.188 \times 200 = 237.60$, and $251.79 - 237.60 = 14.19$.)
**Answer: $\$251.79$**
question.syllabus_check: 4052 percentages and financial mathematics (taxation): successive percentage changes as multipliers, reverse percentage for one stage of a chain, comparing two routes, and a linear equation in one unknown formed from a difference of two totals. No quadratic, no inequality.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q3 was hire purchase, Set 1 P2 Q2 a quadratic from two successive percentage changes with a given final price reversed through the chain, Set 2 P1 Q3 a combined percentage change with a reverse; this Set's P1 Q3 recovers a compound-interest rate and P1 Q7 uses an invariant mass. GCE 2022 P2 Q2 used interest and a card fee on a currency exchange. None of them is a service-charge-then-GST bill with the GST rate change of January 2024, a GST amount recovered from a total, a discount-cancels-the-service-charge misconception explained with multipliers, or a linear equation formed from the difference between a bill under the new rates and the same bill under the old rates. This paper's Q2 forms its equations by balancing two tariffs; (d) here forms one from a stated difference and closes on a forward total, not on the equation. Every number is real-world (Singapore GST 8% to 9% on 1 January 2024).

answers.(c): Kumar is not correct: restaurant (member) costs 0.9 x 1.1 x 1.09 = 1.0791 of the menu price, cafe costs 1.09 of the menu price, so the restaurant is cheaper (by 1.09% of the menu price)

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: 95.92 / 1.09 = 88 exactly, GST = 95.92 - 88 = 7.92; both $7.92. The tempting wrong route 9% of 95.92 = 8.63 is a believable number.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Member at the restaurant 0.9 x 1.1 x 1.09 = 1.0791 of the menu price; cafe 1.09; the restaurant is cheaper, Kumar is wrong. Both say so.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.note: (1.05 x 1.1 x 1.09 - 1.1 x 1.08) x = (1.25895 - 1.188) x = 0.07095 x = 14.19, x = 200 exactly; both $200. The single-6% route gives 236.50 and forgetting the 8% gives 236.70, both plausible.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on every part and I confirm each value; the key is right.
fixes: Lesson 2 (same feel inside the paper): (c) 'Is Kumar correct?' compares two pricing schemes to decide which is cheaper, and the accepted Q2(c) next door also closes by finding where two tariffs give the same bill and which users pay more under the flat rate. Same feel in neighbours. Keep the 0.9 x 1.1 = 0.99 trap but drop the cafe: '(c) Members of the restaurant receive a discount of 10% on the menu price. The service charge and GST are then added to the discounted price. Kumar is a member. He says that, for him, the discount cancels out the service charge, so he pays only the GST on top of the menu price. Explain why Kumar is wrong and find the percentage by which the total a member pays exceeds the menu price. [3]' (answer 7.91%, not 9%; the explanation hangs on 0.9 x 1.1 = 0.99). If the session changes Q2 instead, (c) can stay as it is.

Session note, not a slot defect: every real P2 since 2019 opens with the algebra medley and sets percentages as 1-3-mark parts of the Q2/Q3 medley; an 11-mark money question at Q1 is unlike the real paper's shape. The question itself is at standard.
verdict.why: The repaired question now carries a hidden linear equation in (d)(i) formed from the difference of two three-factor chains (clean answer $200), a reverse step in (b) where the believable wrong answer is 9% of the total, and a comparison in (c) whose reason is a computed fact (0.9 x 1.1 = 0.99); the deciding parts carry 8 of 11 marks, the context changes the maths (GST on the service charge, 8% then 9%), and the wording is SEAB's. Beside Set 1 P2 Q2 it is a little less heavy (a linear rather than a quadratic equation) but as clean, as well built and finishable; the one defect left is the shared 'which scheme is cheaper' feel with Q2(c).

question.stem:
A water supplier charges households $\$a$ for each of the first $20$ m$^3$ of water used in a month and $\$b$ for each additional m$^3$.
To encourage households to save water, the rate for the additional water is the higher rate.
In April a household used $26$ m$^3$ of water and its bill was $\$53.60$.
In May the same household used $35$ m$^3$ of water and its bill was $\$77.00$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
In June the household's bill was $\$100.40$.
Calculate the volume of water, in m$^3$, used in June.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The supplier proposes a new tariff in which every m$^3$ of water costs $\$2.25$, with no higher rate for additional water.
parts.answer: (i) $V = 40$ (ii) households using less than $40$ m$^3$ a month

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: A household uses $V$ m$^3$ of water in a month, where $V > 0$. Its bill is the same under the two tariffs. Find $V$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: Explain which households would pay more under the new tariff.
subparts.answer: Households using less than $40$ m$^3$ a month, because each of the first $20$ m$^3$ costs $\$0.35$ more ($\$7$ in all), and the $\$0.35$ saved on each m$^3$ above $20$ only cancels this once $20$ extra m$^3$ are used (for example $26$ m$^3$: $\$58.50$ under the new tariff instead of $\$53.60$ now).

question.answer: (a) $a = 1.90$, $b = 2.60$ (b) $44$ m$^3$ (c)(i) $V = 40$ (ii) households using less than $40$ m$^3$
skills: form a pair of simultaneous equations from a two-block tariff where the split of each month's volume (20 at one rate, the rest at the other) is not stated: 20a + 6b = 53.60 and 20a + 15b = 77
use the solved rates to find a volume from a bill, deciding that the bill exceeds the cost of the first block so the extra volume is charged at the higher rate

find where a two-block tariff and a flat tariff give the same bill (a linear equation on the second block only, since the first block alone never balances) and read off which users pay more under the flat rate
question.solution:
(a) April: $20$ m$^3$ at $\$a$ and $6$ m$^3$ at $\$b$: $20a + 6b = 53.6$.
May: $20$ m$^3$ at $\$a$ and $15$ m$^3$ at $\$b$: $20a + 15b = 77$.
Subtract: $9b = 23.4$, so $b = 2.6$.
Then $20a = 53.6 - 15.6 = 38$, so $a = 1.9$.
**Answer: $a = 1.90$, $b = 2.60$**

(b) The first $20$ m$^3$ cost $20 \times 1.9 = \$38$, and $100.40 > 38$, so more than $20$ m$^3$ was used.
Additional water: $(100.40 - 38) \div 2.6 = 62.4 \div 2.6 = 24$ m$^3$.
Volume used $= 20 + 24 = 44$.
**Answer: $44$ m$^3$**

(c)(i) For $V \le 20$: $1.9V = 2.25V$ only when $V = 0$, but $V > 0$, so $V > 20$.
Current tariff: $38 + 2.6(V - 20) = 2.6V - 14$.
New tariff: $2.25V$.
$2.6V - 14 = 2.25V$
$0.35V = 14$
$V = 40$
Check: $38 + 2.6 \times 20 = 90 = 2.25 \times 40$.
**Answer: $V = 40$**

(c)(ii) Each of the first $20$ m$^3$ costs $\$2.25$ instead of $\$1.90$: $\$0.35$ more, $\$7$ in all.
Each m$^3$ above $20$ costs $\$2.25$ instead of $\$2.60$: $\$0.35$ less.
The saving only cancels the extra $\$7$ once $20$ extra m$^3$ are used, that is at $40$ m$^3$.
Example: $26$ m$^3$ costs $\$58.50$ under the new tariff but $\$53.60$ now.
**Answer: households using less than $40$ m$^3$ of water a month would pay more.**
question.syllabus_check: 4052 simultaneous linear equations from a word problem, linear equations, utilities bills (financial mathematics). No inequality notation required; no quadratic.
question.originality_note: Earlier simultaneous-equation questions: Set 1 P2 Q1 and Set 2 P2 Q2 (algebraic fractions to a quadratic), Set 1 P1 Q22 (wire cut into edges of two solids), Set 2 P1 Q22 (trimmed mean), Set 1 P1 Q14 (x - y from a rearranged pair); this Set's P1 Q1 forms expressions for coins and P1 Q5 a single linear equation for two candles. Set 2 P1 Q15 compared three gym plans by inequalities in an unknown fee. None uses a two-block tariff whose block split the candidate must see (26 = 20 + 6, 35 = 20 + 15), nor a crossing point between a block tariff and a flat rate with the users who lose identified. Shape of Singapore's increasing-block water tariff, which is real information.
question.marking_note: (c)(ii): "small households" alone earns nothing — the mark needs the 40 m³ threshold, or the $0.35 extra on each of the first 20 m³ set against the $0.35 saved on each m³ above 20.

answers.(c)(ii): Households using less than 35 m^3 of water a month pay more under the new tariff (2.20x > old bill for 0 < x < 35); those using more than 35 m^3 pay less.

issues: (c)(i) Trivially the bills are also equal at 0 m^3 (both $0); the intended non-trivial answer is 35 m^3. Not a real defect, but a marker may want to note 35 is the only positive volume.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.note: 2.6n - 14 = 2.2n gives n = 35; both 35 m^3. The blind examiner rightly notes n = 0 also satisfies 'the same bill' trivially; the wording should exclude it (fix 1).

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.note: Both: households using less than 35 m^3 a month pay more under the flat tariff.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on every part and I confirm each value; the key is right (one cosmetic slip: the key prints the (c) answers twice).
fixes: (c)(i): 'the bill is the same under the two tariffs' is also true at 0 m^3 (both $0); a real paper would close that door. Reword: 'A household uses V m^3 of water in a month, where V > 0. Its bill is the same under the two tariffs. Find V.' — keeps the decision that the first block alone never balances, removes the trivial answer.
Key: the (c) answers are printed twice ('(c) (i) 35 m^3 (ii) households using ...' and again as (c)(i), (c)(ii)); delete the first line.

(c)(ii): SEAB would print 'Explain which households would pay more under the new tariff.' as is, but the marking must demand the 35 m^3 threshold (or the $0.30 extra on each of the first 20 m^3 against $0.40 saved on each m^3 above 20) — 'small households' alone earns nothing.
verdict.why: The context does real work: the 20/6 and 20/15 split is left for the candidate to see (the equations are formed, not cued), (b) needs the decision that $100.40 exceeds the first block, and the flat-tariff break-even needs the old tariff modelled as 2.6n - 14 for n > 20; numbers come out clean (1.90, 2.60, 44, 35) and the explain mark hangs on the computed 35. Nearest earlier work is Set 2 P1 Q15 (cheapest of three plans as inequalities in a fee) — a different skill of the same family, not a repeat; nothing in this paper's Q1 or Q9 shares the skill.

question.stem:
$P$, $Q$ and $R$ are three points on horizontal ground.
$PQ = 60$ m and $PR = 100$ m.
The bearing of $Q$ from $P$ is $070^\circ$ and the bearing of $R$ from $P$ is $190^\circ$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that $QR = 140$ m.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Calculate the bearing of $Q$ from $R$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A vertical tower $PT$ of height $36$ m stands at $P$.
A straight path runs from $Q$ to $R$.
The angle of elevation of $T$ from a point $S$ on the path is $30^\circ$.
Calculate $QS$.

skills: angle between two bearings from one point as an obtuse 120 degrees, then the cosine rule with cos 120 = -1/2 (the sign is the trap) to reach an exact third side
bearing of one point from another through the reverse bearing (190 becomes 010) plus an angle from the sine rule, deciding from the figure whether to add or subtract

locate the point of a straight path from which a tower is seen at a given angle of elevation: the ground distance from the foot of the tower is fixed by the tangent ratio (36/tan 30 = 36 root 3), then that side with PQ and the angle at Q is a two-sides-and-a-non-included-angle triangle, solved by the cosine rule as a quadratic in QS (or the sine rule, angle then side) with the negative root rejected as a point beyond the end of the path
question.figure_description: Not to scale. Plan view of three points on horizontal ground. P is drawn near the middle of the figure with a vertical line through it carrying an upward arrow labelled 'North'. Q is above-right of P (bearing 070 from P, PQ shorter), R is below and slightly left of P (bearing 190 from P, PR longer, about 1.7 times PQ). Straight line segments PQ, PR and QR are drawn, forming triangle PQR with its obtuse angle at P. Label PQ '60 m' and PR '100 m' beside the segments. Mark the bearing of Q from P as a small arc from the north line at P clockwise to PQ labelled '70°', and the bearing of R from P as an arc from the north line clockwise round to PR labelled '190°'. Do NOT show QR's length, any angle at Q or R, a north line at R, the tower, the point S, or any angle of elevation.
question.solution:
(a) Angle $QPR = 190^\circ - 70^\circ = 120^\circ$.
Cosine rule: $QR^2 = 60^2 + 100^2 - 2(60)(100)\cos 120^\circ$
$= 3600 + 10000 - 12000 \times (-0.5)$
$= 3600 + 10000 + 6000 = 19600$.
$QR = \sqrt{19600} = 140$.
**Answer: $QR = 140$ m (shown)**

(b) Sine rule in triangle $PQR$: $\dfrac{\sin \angle PRQ}{60} = \dfrac{\sin 120^\circ}{140}$.
$\sin \angle PRQ = \dfrac{60 \sin 120^\circ}{140} = 0.37115\ldots$, so $\angle PRQ = 21.79^\circ$ (acute, as it is opposite the shortest side).
Bearing of $P$ from $R = 190^\circ - 180^\circ = 010^\circ$.
$Q$ lies clockwise of $RP$ when viewed from $R$, so bearing of $Q$ from $R = 10^\circ + 21.79^\circ = 31.8^\circ$.
**Answer: $031.8^\circ$**

(c) In the right-angled triangle $PST$: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{36}{PS}$, so $PS = \dfrac{36}{\tan 30^\circ} = 36\sqrt{3} = 62.35$ m (and $PS^2 = 3888$).
Angle $PQS = $ angle $PQR = 180^\circ - 120^\circ - 21.79^\circ = 38.21^\circ$ (or $\cos \angle PQR = \dfrac{60^2 + 140^2 - 100^2}{2(60)(140)} = \dfrac{11}{14}$).
Let $QS = x$ m. Cosine rule in triangle $PQS$:
$3888 = 60^2 + x^2 - 2(60)(x)\cos 38.21^\circ$
$x^2 - 94.29x - 288 = 0$
$x = \dfrac{94.29 \pm \sqrt{94.29^2 + 4(288)}}{2} = \dfrac{94.29 \pm 100.21}{2}$
$x = 97.25$ or $x = -2.96$.
$QS$ cannot be negative (that point is on $RQ$ produced, not on the path), so $QS = 97.2$ m.
**Answer: $QS = 97.2$ m**

Alternative for (c) by the sine rule: $\dfrac{\sin \angle PSQ}{60} = \dfrac{\sin 38.21^\circ}{62.35}$, so $\sin \angle PSQ = 0.5952$ and $\angle PSQ = 36.53^\circ$ (the obtuse value $143.47^\circ$ exceeds $180^\circ - 38.21^\circ$).
Angle $QPS = 180^\circ - 38.21^\circ - 36.53^\circ = 105.26^\circ$.
$QS = \dfrac{62.35 \sin 105.26^\circ}{\sin 38.21^\circ} = 97.2$ m.

Check: $QS = 97.2 < 140$, so $S$ is on the path. The nearest point of the path to $P$ is $47.1$ m from $Q$ at $37.1$ m from $P$ (elevation $44.1^\circ$); the elevation at $Q$ itself is $\tan^{-1}(36/60) = 31.0^\circ$ and at $R$ is $19.8^\circ$, so $30^\circ$ is reached at exactly one point of the path, on the $R$ side of the nearest point.
Tidy wrong answers: $\sqrt{PS^2 - PQ^2} = 17.0$ m (a right angle assumed at $S$); $62.4$ m (giving $PS$ as $QS$).
Marking: (a) M1 for $120^\circ$ and the cosine rule set up, A1 $140$. (b) M1 sine rule for angle $PRQ$ ($21.8^\circ$), M1 reverse bearing $010^\circ$ or equivalent, A1 $031.8^\circ$. (c) M1 $PS = 36/\tan 30^\circ$, M1 the angle at $Q$ (from (b) or $\cos Q = 11/14$), M1 a correct equation for $QS$ (the cosine-rule quadratic, or the sine rule for angle $PSQ$ then angle $QPS$), A1 $97.2$ with the negative root rejected.

question.stem:
The speed limit on a road is 60 km/h.

The speeds, in km/h, of 200 cars passing a point on the road were recorded in one week in January.

A speed camera was then installed at this point.

The speeds of 200 cars passing the same point were recorded in one week in March.

The cumulative frequency curves show the speeds of the cars in January and in March.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Use the January curve to find

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: the interquartile range of the speeds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A driver travelling at more than 20 km/h above the speed limit has their driving licence suspended.

A driver travelling above the speed limit, but not more than 20 km/h above it, is given a warning.

Find, in its simplest form, the ratio of the number of drivers given a warning in January to the number of drivers whose licence was suspended in January.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Before the speed camera was installed, the town council set two targets for the speeds of the cars in March.

Target 1: no more than 5% of the cars travelling at speeds greater than $V$ km/h.

Target 2: a median speed at least 5 km/h below the speed limit.

In January, 20% of the cars were travelling at speeds greater than $V$ km/h.

Determine whether each target was met in March.

Justify your answers using figures from the curves.
parts.answer: $V = 70$. Target 1 not met: in March $200 - 186 = 14$ cars, which is $7\%$ (accept 6.5% to 7.5%), were faster than 70 km/h, more than 5%. Target 2 met: the March median is about 53 km/h (accept 52 to 54), which is about 7 km/h below 60 km/h, at least 5 km/h below the limit.

skills: two cumulative frequency curves on one grid for the same road before and after a speed camera: the drivers in the band from the speed limit to 20 km/h above it counted as the difference of two readings (not the reading itself), then set in a ratio against the drivers above the band

a percentile found on one curve (the speed exceeded by 20% of the January cars, cumulative frequency 160, not 40) and carried across to the other curve to read the proportion above that speed in March, then judged against a 5% target

two stated targets judged from the curves with no statistic named for the candidate: a proportion above a speed (met or not met) and a median at least 5 km/h below the speed limit, each decision justified with the figures read
question.figure_description:
ONE figure: a graph grid of 2 mm squares, 12 cm wide by 20 cm tall, with TWO cumulative frequency curves already drawn on it.

Horizontal axis labelled 'Speed (km/h)', running from 40 to 100, with 2 cm representing 10 km/h (so 2 mm = 1 km/h) and the values 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100 printed at the 2 cm lines. Vertical axis labelled 'Cumulative frequency', running from 0 to 200, with 2 cm representing 20 (so 2 mm = 2) and the values 0, 20, 40, ..., 200 printed at the 2 cm lines. The axes meet at (40, 0).

Curve 1, labelled 'January': a smooth increasing curve through EVERY one of these points, in order: (40, 0), (45, 4), (50, 16), (55, 50), (60, 100), (64, 128), (67, 147), (70, 160), (73, 168), (76, 174), (80, 180), (85, 188), (90, 194), (95, 198), (100, 200). Draw it as a single smooth curve (a monotone curve through the points, no straight segments, no overshoot between points); it is steepest between 55 and 60 and flattens towards (100, 200). The points (55, 50), (60, 100), (70, 160) and (80, 180) are the readings, and the curve reads about 150 at 68, the question depends on: the curve must pass through each of them exactly.

Curve 2, labelled 'March': a smooth increasing curve through EVERY one of these points, in order: (40, 0), (45, 20), (50, 60), (53, 100), (55, 120), (60, 150), (65, 174), (70, 186), (75, 192), (80, 196), (85, 199), (90, 200), (95, 200), (100, 200). Draw it as a single smooth monotone curve, no straight segments, no overshoot; it is steepest between 50 and 60, lies to the LEFT of (above) the January curve everywhere between 40 and 90, and runs level at 200 from 90 to 100. The points (53, 100) and (70, 186) are the readings the question depends on: the curve must pass through each of them exactly.

Both curves are solid black lines of the same weight. The word 'January' is printed just below and to the right of the January curve at about (74, 130); the word 'March' is printed just above and to the left of the March curve at about (43, 110). The two curves must be clearly distinguishable where they approach each other near the top right.

No plotted points are marked with dots or crosses. No frequencies, quartiles, percentiles, horizontal or vertical reading lines, or any other values appear on the figure. Nothing is shaded.
question.solution:
(a)(i) The median is the 100th value.

On the January curve, cumulative frequency 100 is at 60 km/h.

**Answer: 60 km/h**

(a)(ii) Lower quartile: the 50th value. From the January curve, 55 km/h.

Upper quartile: the 150th value. From the January curve, 68 km/h.

Interquartile range $= 68 - 55 = 13$ km/h.

**Answer: about 13 km/h (accept 12 to 14)**

(b) 20 km/h above the limit is 80 km/h.

A warning: more than 60 km/h and not more than 80 km/h.

A suspension: more than 80 km/h.

January curve at 60 km/h: cumulative frequency 100.

January curve at 80 km/h: cumulative frequency 180.

Warnings $= 180 - 100 = 80$.

Suspensions $= 200 - 180 = 20$.

Ratio $= 80 : 20 = 4 : 1$.

**Answer: $4 : 1$**

(c) Target 1.

20% of 200 cars is 40 cars.

So in January 160 cars were travelling at $V$ km/h or slower.

January curve at cumulative frequency 160: $V = 70$.

March curve at 70 km/h: cumulative frequency 186.

Cars faster than 70 km/h in March $= 200 - 186 = 14$.

$\frac{14}{200} \times 100\% = 7\%$

$7\% > 5\%$, so Target 1 was not met.

Target 2.

At least 5 km/h below the limit means a median of 55 km/h or less.

March median: the 100th value. From the March curve, about 53 km/h.

$60 - 53 = 7$ km/h below the limit, so Target 2 was met.

**Answer: Target 1 not met (7% of the March cars were faster than 70 km/h, more than 5%); Target 2 met (March median about 53 km/h, about 7 km/h below 60 km/h).**

(Marking: (a)(i) B1 60. (a)(ii) M1 both quartiles read (lower 54 to 55.5, upper 67 to 68.5), A1 12 to 14. (b) M1 the boundaries 60 and 80 identified and both readings taken (99 to 101, 179 to 181); M1 the counts 80 and 20 by subtraction; A1 $4 : 1$. Taking 180 as the number warned, giving $9 : 1$, scores M1 only. (c) M1 reading the January curve at cumulative frequency 160 to give $V = 70$ (accept 69.5 to 70.5); M1 the March reading at $V$ (185 to 187) subtracted from 200, giving 13 to 15 cars; A1 6.5% to 7.5% with the conclusion that Target 1 was not met; B1 March median 52 to 54; A1 the median compared with 55 (or the gap 6 to 8 km/h stated against 5) with the conclusion that Target 2 was met. Reading at cumulative frequency 40 ($V \approx 54$, about 45% in March) scores 0 for the first three marks. A decision with no figure quoted earns no A mark; 'the March curve is further left' alone scores 0.)

Ratio in its simplest form and a percentage are Sec 1 number work. No mean, no standard deviation, no probability, no histogram. Every reading the key depends on sits on a stated point of a curve: January (55, 50), (60, 100), (68, 150), (70, 160), (80, 180); March (53, 100), (70, 186).

question.stem:
A patient is given a 50 mg dose of a medicine.

The amount, $y$ mg, of the medicine remaining in the patient's blood $x$ hours after the dose is given by

$y = 50 \times 0.8^{x}$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text:
The table shows some values of $x$ and the corresponding values of $y$, correct to 1 decimal place.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline y & 50 & 40 & 32 & 25.6 & 20.5 & 16.4 & 13.1 & & 8.4 \\ \hline \end{array}$

Complete the table.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: On the grid, draw the graph of $y = 50 \times 0.8^{x}$ for $0 \le x \le 8$.
subparts.answer: Smooth decreasing curve through the nine points, falling more and more slowly

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A second patient is given a 50 mg dose of a different medicine at the same time.

The amount of this medicine in the blood falls by the same amount every hour, and 3.5 hours after the dose exactly half of it remains.

By drawing a suitable straight line on the grid, find how many hours after the doses the amounts of the two medicines remaining in the blood are next equal.
parts.answer: Straight line from $(0, 50)$ to $(7, 0)$; the line crosses the curve again at $x \approx 4.35$, so about 4.35 hours after the doses (accept 4.25 to 4.45)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
By drawing a tangent, estimate the rate at which the amount of the first medicine in the blood is decreasing at the time when 30 mg of it remains.

State the units of your answer.
parts.answer: Tangent at the point where $y = 30$ (about $x = 2.3$); gradient $\approx -6.7$, so the amount is decreasing at about 6.7 mg per hour (accept 5.8 to 7.6 mg per hour)

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Use your graph to find the greatest difference between the amounts of the two medicines in the blood during the first 4 hours after the doses.
parts.answer: About 3.7 mg, at about 2 hours after the doses (accept 3.4 to 4.0 mg)

skills: a second process described only in words (constant rate, none left after 7 hours) turned, unprompted, into the straight line through $(0, 50)$ and $(7, 0)$ on the same grid, and the next time the two amounts are equal read from where that line crosses the drawn decay curve (the word 'next' in the question sets the common start aside)
gradient by a tangent at a point the candidate must first locate from its $y$-value (30 mg remaining, about $x = 2.3$), the result reported as a rate of decrease with its units, mg per hour

greatest vertical gap between the drawn line and the drawn curve over an interval, read by scanning the gap (or by seeing it is widest where the tangent is parallel to the line), the tempting wrong readings being the gap at an end of the interval
question.figure_description: A blank graph grid of 2 mm squares, 16 cm wide by 20 cm tall, for part (a)(ii). Horizontal axis labelled '$x$ (hours)' running from 0 to 8, with 2 cm representing 1 hour and the integers 0 to 8 printed at the 2 cm lines. Vertical axis labelled '$y$ (mg)' running from 0 to 50, with 2 cm representing 5 mg and the values 0, 5, 10, ..., 50 printed at the 2 cm lines. The axes meet at the origin. NOTHING is drawn on the grid: no points, no curve, no line, no tangent, no equation.
question.solution:
(a)(i) $x = 7$: $y = 50 \times 0.8^{7} = 50 \times 0.2097\ldots = 10.49\ldots = 10.5$ (1 d.p.)

**Answer: $10.5$**

(a)(ii) Plot the nine points $(0, 50)$, $(1, 40)$, $(2, 32)$, $(3, 25.6)$, $(4, 20.5)$, $(5, 16.4)$, $(6, 13.1)$, $(7, 10.5)$, $(8, 8.4)$ and join them with a smooth curve that falls more and more slowly.

**Answer: smooth decreasing curve through the nine points**

(b) The second medicine starts at 50 mg and falls by the same amount each hour, from 50 mg to 25 mg in 3.5 hours, so it reaches 0 mg at 7 hours.

So its amount is a straight line from $(0, 50)$ to $(7, 0)$, that is $y = 50 - \frac{50}{7}x$.

Draw this line on the grid.

The line and the curve meet at $x = 0$ (both amounts are 50 mg at the start) and again where the line crosses the curve: from the graph, at $x \approx 4.35$.

(Check: at $x = 4.35$, $50 \times 0.8^{4.35} = 18.9$ and $50 - \frac{50}{7}(4.35) = 18.9$.)

**Answer: about $4.35$ hours after the doses (accept 4.25 to 4.45)**

(c) When 30 mg remains, $y = 30$: from the curve this is at $x \approx 2.3$.

Draw the tangent to the curve at this point and find its gradient from two points on the tangent, for example $(0, 45.3)$ and $(6, 5.2)$.

Gradient $\approx \frac{5.2 - 45.3}{6 - 0} = -6.7$

(Exact: $x = \frac{\lg 0.6}{\lg 0.8} = 2.29$ and the gradient there is $30 \ln 0.8 = -6.69$.)

**Answer: the amount is decreasing at about $6.7$ mg per hour (accept 5.8 to 7.6 mg per hour)**

(d) In the first 4 hours the line is above the curve (they next meet at 4.35 hours), so the difference is the vertical gap from the curve up to the line.

From the graph the gap is widest at about $x = 2$: line $50 - \frac{50}{7}(2) = 35.7$, curve $32$, gap $3.7$.

(Check: the gap is $3.5$ at $x = 1.5$ and at $x = 2.5$, $2.9$ at $x = 1$ and at $x = 3$, $0.9$ at $x = 4$; it is widest where the tangent to the curve is parallel to the line, which is at $x = 2.00$.)

**Answer: about $3.7$ mg (accept 3.4 to 4.0)**

(b) L1 straight line from $(0, 50)$ to $(7, 0)$; A1 $x$ in $4.25$ to $4.45$; $x = 0$ alone scores 0. (c) T1 tangent drawn at the point where $y = 30$, touching the curve there and not crossing it (a tangent at $x = 3$ or at $y = 20$ scores T0); M1 gradient from two points on the tangent, at least 3 cm apart; A1 magnitude in $5.8$ to $7.6$ with the unit mg per hour (a negative gradient with the unit, or a positive value with 'decreasing', is accepted; a value with no unit loses A1). question.stem:
The diagram shows a container that is open at the top.

The top of the container is a horizontal square of side 32 cm and the base is a horizontal square of side 20 cm. The centre of the top is vertically above the centre of the base.

The four sloping faces are congruent trapeziums.

The vertical height of the container is 24 cm.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the capacity of the container is $16\,512$ cm$^3$.
parts.answer: Apex of the completed pyramid is 40 cm below the base ($\frac{20}{32} = \frac{h}{h + 24}$); capacity $= \frac{1}{3}(32^2)(64) - \frac{1}{3}(20^2)(40) = \frac{65536}{3} - \frac{16000}{3} = 16\,512$ cm$^3$

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The outside of the four sloping faces of the container is to be painted.

Calculate the total area to be painted.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The container stands on horizontal ground and water is poured into it at a constant rate.

After 36 seconds, the depth of the water is 8 cm.

Calculate the time taken to fill the container completely.

Give your answer in minutes and seconds, correct to the nearest second.
parts.answer: 2 minutes 33 seconds (water at depth 8 cm has volume $\frac{1}{3}(24^2)(48) - \frac{16000}{3} = 3882.67$ cm$^3$; rate $= 107.85$ cm$^3$/s; $16512 \div 107.85 = 153.1$ s)

skills: capacity of an open container with a 32 cm square top, a 20 cm square base and height 24 cm found by completing the pyramid: the apex 40 cm below the base by similar triangles, then one pyramid volume minus another
area of the four sloping trapezium faces using the face's own slant height $\sqrt{24^2 + 6^2}$ (half the difference of the sides, not the vertical height and not the slant edge)

constant-rate filling: the water at depth 8 cm is itself the difference of two pyramids (surface a 24 cm square), so the rate comes from that volume and the filling time is not proportional to the depth
question.figure_description: A 3-D drawing of a container shaped like a square-based pyramid with its top cut off and turned so that the WIDER square is at the top: an open-topped square 'tub' whose sides slope outwards going up. The top is a horizontal square of side 32 cm (drawn in perspective as a parallelogram, all four edges solid since the top is open), the base is a smaller horizontal square of side 20 cm directly below it (front edge solid, back edges dashed), and four sloping trapezium faces join corresponding edges. Label the front top edge '32 cm' and the front base edge '20 cm'. Draw a dashed vertical line from the centre of the base to the centre of the top and label it '24 cm'. Do NOT draw the apex or any extension of the sloping edges below the base, do NOT mark any slant height, slant edge, water level or volume. Caption: Not drawn to scale.
question.solution:
(a) Extend the four sloping edges downwards: they meet at a point $V$ below the base, because the top and base are similar squares with the same centre.

Let $V$ be $h$ cm below the base. Then $V$ is $(h + 24)$ cm below the top.

By similar triangles (the half-widths 10 and 16 against the heights),

$\frac{h}{h + 24} = \frac{20}{32}$

$32h = 20h + 480$

$h = 40$

The container is the pyramid of base 32 cm and height $64$ cm with the pyramid of base 20 cm and height 40 cm removed.

Capacity $= \frac{1}{3}(32)^2(64) - \frac{1}{3}(20)^2(40)$

$= \frac{65536}{3} - \frac{16000}{3}$

$= \frac{49536}{3}$

$= 16\,512$ cm$^3$ (shown)

**Answer: capacity $= 16\,512$ cm$^3$**

(b) Each sloping face is a trapezium with parallel sides 32 cm and 20 cm.

The height of the trapezium is the slant height of the face, from the midpoint of a base edge to the midpoint of the top edge above it.

Horizontally the top edge is $\frac{32 - 20}{2} = 6$ cm beyond the base edge; vertically it is 24 cm higher.

Slant height $= \sqrt{24^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{612} = 24.74$ cm (4 s.f.)

Area of one face $= \frac{1}{2}(32 + 20)(24.74) = 643.2$ cm$^2$

Area to be painted $= 4 \times 643.2 = 2572.8$ cm$^2$

**Answer: $2570$ cm$^2$**

(c) At depth 8 cm the water surface is a horizontal square $40 + 8 = 48$ cm above $V$.

Side of the water surface $= 48 \times \frac{32}{64} = 24$ cm

Volume of water $= \frac{1}{3}(24)^2(48) - \frac{1}{3}(20)^2(40) = 9216 - \frac{16000}{3} = 3882.67$ cm$^3$

Rate of pouring $= \frac{3882.67}{36} = 107.85$ cm$^3$ per second

Time to fill the container $= \frac{16512}{107.85} = 153.1$ s

$153.1$ s $= 2$ minutes $33$ seconds

**Answer: 2 minutes 33 seconds**

(Marking: (a) M1 similar triangles giving an equation for the apex distance, A1 $h = 40$ (or whole height 64), M1 difference of the two pyramid volumes, A1 $16\,512$ reached exactly. The frustum formula $\frac{24}{3}(1024 + 400 + 640)$ earns full marks. (b) M1 slant height $\sqrt{612}$, M1 $4 \times \frac{1}{2}(52)(\text{their slant})$, A1 $2570$ to $2573$. Using 24 as the trapezium height gives 2496 and earns M0 M1 A0. (c) M1 water surface side 24 cm (or height 48 above $V$), M1 water volume as a difference of pyramids, A1 $3882.67$ or $3880$, M1 rate then $16512 \div$ their rate, A1 2 min 33 s. Taking the time as proportional to the depth ($36 \times 3 = 108$ s $= 1$ min 48 s) scores 0.)
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Mensuration: volume of a pyramid $\frac{1}{3} \times$ base area $\times$ height (formula sheet), a solid with a part removed treated by subtraction, area of a trapezium, rate of filling as volume per second. Congruence and similarity: corresponding lengths of similar figures (the completed pyramid and the removed pyramid). Pythagoras' theorem for the slant height. No frustum formula is required, no cone, no sphere, no trigonometry.
question.originality_note: An open square 'tub' that is a square pyramid with its top removed and turned wide side up: not this Set's P1 Q22 (a cylinder with a conical hollow, in terms of $\pi$), not Set 1 P1 Q26 (a complete pyramid from angle $VAO$) or Set 1 P1 Q22 (wire edges of a cuboid and a pyramid), not Set 1 P2 Q9 (cylinder tanks and rainfall in litres), not Set 2 P1 Q26 (pipe flow into an aquarium with a sphere inside), not Set 2 P1 Q27 (a trapezium cut by vectors). Against the real papers: GCE 2025 P2 Q6(b) melts a pyramid into cubes and a sphere; GCE 2024 P1 Q26 and GCE 2025 P1 Q21 fill a cone or cone-and-cylinder with water and ask for a depth by cube roots; GCE 2024 P2 Q9 makes candles from similar cylinders. Here nothing names a pyramid: the candidate must see the completed pyramid in (a), must find the face's slant height through the 6 cm offset in (b) (using 24 cm gives a tidy wrong 2496), and in (c) must see that the water at 8 cm is again a difference of pyramids before any rate exists (the proportional answer 1 min 48 s is the trap). Closing step: a filling time in minutes and seconds from a rate, unlike the graph readings of Q4 and Q5. The 5-mark part chains similar triangles, two volumes, a rate and a division with no intermediate value supplied, as the paper plan assigns to Q6.

parts.note: Both 2570 cm^2 (2572.8; 104 sqrt(612)). Slant height sqrt(24^2 + 6^2) = 24.74, face 643.2, four faces 2572.8.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both 2 min 33 s. Water surface at depth 8 cm is a 24 cm square (48 above the apex, scale 1/2); volume 9216 - 16000/3 = 3882.67; rate 107.85 cm^3/s; 16512 / 107.85 = 153.1 s.

question.stem:
The diagram shows a sector $OAB$ of a circle, centre $O$ and radius 12 cm.
Angle $AOB = \frac{\pi}{3}$ radians.
A circle, centre $C$, lies inside the sector. It touches $OA$ at $P$, $OB$ at $Q$ and the arc $AB$ at $T$.
The region bounded by $OP$, $OQ$ and the minor arc $PQ$ is shaded.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the radius of the circle with centre $C$ is 4 cm.
parts.answer: $r = 4$ (shown): $O$, $C$, $T$ collinear so $OC = 12 - r$; $OC$ bisects angle $AOB$ so angle $POC = \frac{\pi}{6}$; $\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{r}{12 - r}$ gives $12 - r = 2r$, $r = 4$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Calculate the area of the shaded region.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A smaller circle is drawn inside the shaded region so that it touches $OP$, $OQ$ and the circle with centre $C$.
Find the exact radius of this smaller circle.

skills: radius of a circle inscribed in a sector: the line of centres through the point of contact gives OC = R - r, the bisector gives the half-angle, and sin(half-angle) = r/(R - r) in the right-angled triangle at the tangent point

area between two tangents from a point and the minor arc between the points of contact: kite minus sector, the angle at the centre of the small circle coming from the angle sum of the quadrilateral with two right angles
radius of a second circle nested between the first circle and the vertex of the sector, by reusing the half-angle relation along the bisector and adding the distances along it
question.figure_description: A sector OAB of a circle with centre O and radius 12 cm, drawn with O at the bottom left. For the drawer, take O = (0, 0), A = (12, 0) so that OA is horizontal to the right, and B = (6, 10.39) so that OB makes 60 degrees with OA; draw the straight radii OA and OB and the arc from A to B (anticlockwise, bulging away from O). Inside the sector draw a circle with centre C = (6.93, 4) and radius 4: it touches OA at P = (6.93, 0), touches OB at Q = (3.46, 6) and touches the arc AB at T = (10.39, 6). Mark C with a small dot. Label the points O, A, B, C, P, Q and T beside their positions (O at the vertex, A at the right end of the horizontal radius, B at the top end of the slanted radius, P on OA, Q on OB, T on the arc, C at the centre of the circle). Print the length '12 cm' beside OA and mark the angle at O with a small arc labelled 'pi/3' (set as $\frac{\pi}{3}$). Shade (light grey) ONLY the curvilinear triangle at the vertex O, bounded by the segment OP, the segment OQ and the minor arc of the circle from P to Q (the arc nearer to O). Do not draw CP, CQ, OC or OT, do not print the radius of the circle or any angle other than pi/3, and do not draw the smaller circle of part (c). Note 'Not drawn to scale' is NOT needed; the figure may be to scale.
question.solution:
(a)
The circle touches the arc $AB$ at $T$, so $O$, $C$ and $T$ lie on a straight line (the centres of two touching circles and the point of contact are collinear).
$OC = OT - CT = 12 - r$, where $r$ is the radius of the circle.
$OP = OQ$ (tangents from $O$), so $OC$ bisects angle $AOB$: angle $POC = \frac{\pi}{6}$.
$CP$ is perpendicular to $OA$ (tangent perpendicular to radius).
In triangle $OPC$: $\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{CP}{OC} = \frac{r}{12 - r}$.
$\frac{1}{2}(12 - r) = r$
$12 - r = 2r$
$r = 4$
**Answer:** radius $= 4$ cm (shown).

(b)
$OC = 12 - 4 = 8$ cm.
$OP = \sqrt{8^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}$ cm (Pythagoras in triangle $OPC$).
Area of kite $OPCQ = 2 \times \frac{1}{2} \times OP \times CP = 4\sqrt{3} \times 4 = 16\sqrt{3}$ cm$^2$.
In quadrilateral $OPCQ$, angles $OPC$ and $OQC$ are right angles, so angle $PCQ = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3}$.
Area of sector $CPQ = \frac{1}{2} \times 4^2 \times \frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{16\pi}{3}$ cm$^2$.
Shaded area $= 16\sqrt{3} - \frac{16\pi}{3} = 27.71 - 16.76 = 10.96$ cm$^2$.
**Answer:** $11.0$ cm$^2$.

(c)
Let the smaller circle have centre $D$ and radius $x$ cm.
By symmetry $D$ lies on $OC$, and as in (a), $\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{x}{OD}$, so $OD = 2x$.
The two circles touch, so $DC = x + 4$.
$OD + DC = OC$: $2x + x + 4 = 8$
$3x = 4$
$x = \frac{4}{3}$
**Answer:** $\frac{4}{3}$ cm.
question.syllabus_check: 4052: arc, sector and segment work with the angle in radians (Circular Measure); tangent perpendicular to radius, equal tangents from an external point, two circles touching (Circle Properties); sine in a right-angled triangle and Pythagoras' theorem (Trigonometry). No calculus, no surds beyond an exact intermediate 4 root 3 that the candidate may keep as a decimal.
question.originality_note: A circle inscribed in a sector, with the region at the vertex shaded and a second nested circle to close. Not a chord-and-segment cross-section (Set 1 P2 Q8 tunnel), not a belt round two pulleys (Set 2 P2 Q8), not a sector scaled by area (Set 1 P1 Q2), not radius from arc and area (Set 2 P1 Q9); not the two intersecting circles of GCE 2024 P2 Q8(b) nor the tangent-and-chord perimeter of GCE 2023 P2 Q5. The show-that is built by the candidate (collinear centres, bisector, sine); the area is a kite minus a sector of the SMALL circle with its angle deduced, not sector minus triangle of the big circle; the closing part reuses the half-angle relation in a new way.

answers.(a): shown (OC = r / sin(pi/6) = 2r; OC + r = 12 so 3r = 12, r = 4 cm)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both reach r = 4 by the same route: O, C, T collinear so OC = 12 - r, OC bisects the pi/3 angle, sin(pi/6) = r/(12 - r). Checked: 12 - r = 2r, r = 4.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 16 sqrt(3) - 16 pi/3 = 10.96, i.e. 11.0 cm^2. Checked: OP = sqrt(64 - 16) = 4 sqrt(3), kite OPCQ = 16 sqrt(3), angle PCQ = 2 pi - pi/2 - pi/2 - pi/3 = 2 pi/3, sector = (1/2)(16)(2 pi/3) = 16 pi/3.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both give 4/3 cm. Checked: the nested circle's centre D is on OC with OD = 2x (same half-angle relation), DC = x + 4, OD + DC = OC = 8 gives 3x = 4.

verdict.why: Every part needs its own idea (the line of centres through T so OC = 12 - r; the kite-minus-sector decomposition with angle PCQ from the quadrilateral; reusing the half-angle relation along the bisector for the nested circle), the wrong decision in (a) (OC = 12) lands on the tidy r = 6, the numbers come out exact (4, 4 sqrt(3), 4/3), and nothing in the stem names a rule. No 2024/25 question has this situation (GCE 2024 P2 Q8(b) is two intersecting circles, sector minus triangle); no earlier Set has a circle inscribed in a sector or a nested-circle sting (Set 1 P2 Q5 found an incircle radius from area and perimeter; Set 2 P2 Q8 used a common external tangent of two separate circles); nothing in this paper so far uses the tangent-kite or the half-angle relation. Beside Set 1 P2 Q8 (show r [3], then an area, then a sting) it is as demanding, cleaner in its numbers and ends on an exact 2-mark sting that uses (a) in a new way.

question.stem:
In the diagram, $OAB$ is a triangle with $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$.
$C$ is the point on $OA$ such that $OC : CA = 3 : 2$ and $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$.
The line $CD$ is produced to meet $OB$ produced at the point $E$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The line $CD$ divides triangle $OAB$ into two parts.
Find the ratio of the area of triangle $ACD$ to the area of quadrilateral $OCDB$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the ratio $OB : BE$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
$G$ is the point on $OE$ such that $OG : GE = 2 : 1$.
What type of quadrilateral is $ADGE$? Justify your answer using vectors.
parts.answer: Trapezium: $\overrightarrow{DG} = \frac{1}{2}(3\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) = \frac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AE}$, so $DG$ is parallel to $AE$ but $DG \ne AE$ (and $AD$ is not parallel to $GE$), so exactly one pair of opposite sides is parallel

question.answer: (a) $1 : 4$; (b) $OB : BE = 1 : 2$; (c) trapezium, since $\overrightarrow{DG} = \frac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AE}$ (one pair of opposite sides parallel and unequal)
skills: ratio of the two pieces into which a line from a point on one side to the midpoint of another cuts a triangle, with no area given: two common-height ratios chosen by the candidate (ACD : OCD = CA : OC from the shared apex D, then OAD = OBD from the midpoint) and the quadrilateral assembled as a sum, so 2 : 3 and 1 : 5 are the tempting wrong answers

two-parameter collinearity with the unknown point on a side produced and no parameter printed: the candidate builds CD, writes OE = k b and CE = m CD unprompted, equates the coefficients of a and b, and reads OB : BE from k

identify a quadrilateral from vectors: show one pair of opposite sides parallel by DG = half of AE, and say why unequal parallel sides make it a trapezium and not a parallelogram (the point G given as a 2 : 1 point of OE, so the candidate must first use OE = 3b)
question.figure_description: A triangle OAB, not to scale, with O at the bottom left. For the drawer, take O = (0, 0), A = (10, 0) to the right, B = (4, 5) above and to the right of O, and E = (12, 15) on OB produced beyond B (so that OE = 3 OB). Mark C on OA at (6, 0) (three-fifths of the way from O to A) and D at (7, 2.5), the midpoint of AB. Draw the segment OA, the segment AB, ONE straight line from O through B to E, and ONE straight line from C through D to E (the line CD produced meets OB produced at E). Label the points O, A, B, C, D and E beside their positions (C below OA, D to the right of AB, E at the top right). Mark the vector a with an arrowhead along OA pointing from O to A and label it with a bold lower-case a; mark the vector b with an arrowhead along OB pointing from O to B and label it with a bold lower-case b. Do NOT mark the point G, do NOT draw the segments AE, DG or OD, and do not print any ratio, length or area.
question.solution:
(a)
Triangles $ACD$ and $OCD$ have the same height from $D$ to the line $OA$, and $CA : OC = 2 : 3$.
Area of triangle $ACD$ : area of triangle $OCD = 2 : 3$.
Take area of triangle $ACD = 2$ units and area of triangle $OCD = 3$ units, so area of triangle $OAD = 5$ units.
Triangles $OAD$ and $OBD$ have the same height from $O$ to the line $AB$, and $AD = DB$.
Area of triangle $OBD = $ area of triangle $OAD = 5$ units.
Area of quadrilateral $OCDB = $ area of triangle $OCD + $ area of triangle $OBD = 3 + 5 = 8$ units.
Area of triangle $ACD$ : area of quadrilateral $OCDB = 2 : 8$.
**Answer:** $1 : 4$

(b)
$\overrightarrow{OC} = \frac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}$
$\overrightarrow{OD} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b})$
$\overrightarrow{CD} = \overrightarrow{OD} - \overrightarrow{OC} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b} - \frac{3}{5}\mathbf{a} = -\frac{1}{10}\mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b} = \frac{1}{10}(5\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$
$E$ lies on $OB$ produced, so $\overrightarrow{OE} = k\mathbf{b}$ for some number $k$.
$C$, $D$ and $E$ lie on one straight line, so $\overrightarrow{CE} = m\overrightarrow{CD}$ for some number $m$.
$\overrightarrow{CE} = \overrightarrow{OE} - \overrightarrow{OC} = k\mathbf{b} - \frac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}$
$k\mathbf{b} - \frac{3}{5}\mathbf{a} = \frac{m}{10}(5\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$
Comparing $\mathbf{a}$: $-\frac{3}{5} = -\frac{m}{10}$, so $m = 6$.
Comparing $\mathbf{b}$: $k = \frac{5m}{10} = 3$.
$\overrightarrow{OE} = 3\mathbf{b}$, so $\overrightarrow{BE} = 3\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{b} = 2\mathbf{b}$.
(Or, with one parameter: $\overrightarrow{OE} = \overrightarrow{OC} + m\overrightarrow{CD} = \left(\frac{3}{5} - \frac{m}{10}\right)\mathbf{a} + \frac{m}{2}\mathbf{b}$, and $E$ on $OB$ needs the coefficient of $\mathbf{a}$ to be $0$, so $m = 6$ and $\overrightarrow{OE} = 3\mathbf{b}$.)
**Answer:** $OB : BE = 1 : 2$

(c)
$\overrightarrow{OG} = \frac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{OE} = \frac{2}{3}(3\mathbf{b}) = 2\mathbf{b}$
$\overrightarrow{DG} = \overrightarrow{OG} - \overrightarrow{OD} = 2\mathbf{b} - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b} = \frac{3}{2}\mathbf{b} - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} = \frac{1}{2}(3\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$
$\overrightarrow{AE} = \overrightarrow{OE} - \overrightarrow{OA} = 3\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$
$\overrightarrow{DG} = \frac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AE}$, so $DG$ is parallel to $AE$ and $DG = \frac{1}{2}AE$.
$DG$ and $AE$ are a pair of opposite sides of $ADGE$ that are parallel but not equal in length, so $ADGE$ is not a parallelogram.
(Check of the other pair: $\overrightarrow{AD} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$ and $\overrightarrow{GE} = \mathbf{b}$ are not multiples of each other, so $AD$ is not parallel to $GE$.)
**Answer:** $ADGE$ is a trapezium, because $\overrightarrow{DG} = \frac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AE}$: one pair of opposite sides is parallel and they are unequal

No dot product, no 3-D, no midpoint theorem required.

answers.(c): Trapezium: DG = (3b - a)/2 = 1/2 AE where AE = 3b - a, so DG is parallel to AE (and half its length); AD = (b - a)/2 is not parallel to GE = b, so exactly one pair of parallel sides

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 1 : 4. Checked: ACD : OCD = CA : OC = 2 : 3 (shared apex D, bases on OA); OAD = OBD (D the midpoint of AB, apex O), so OAD = 5 units, OBD = 5, OCDB = 3 + 5 = 8, ACD : OCDB = 2 : 8. Coordinates O(0,0) A(10,0) B(4,5) C(6,0) D(7,2.5) confirm it: ACD = 5, OCDB = 20. The tempting wrong answers 2 : 3 and 1 : 5 are real.

parts.note: Both OB : BE = 1 : 2. Checked: CD = -(1/10)a + (1/2)b; OE = OC + m CD = (3/5 - m/10)a + (m/2)b, and E on OB needs the a-coefficient zero, so m = 6 and OE = 3b, BE = 2b. Coordinates: C(6,0) + 6(1, 2.5) = (12, 15) = 3B. Exactly right.

With A(10,0) D(7,2.5) G(8,10) E(12,15) the vertex order A-D-G-E is a convex simple quadrilateral (all four edge cross-products negative), DG parallel to AE and half its length, the other pair not parallel - exactly one pair of parallel sides, so a trapezium and not a parallelogram. verdict.why: Every part hands the candidate a decision and all 10 marks sit in deciding parts: (a) an area ratio with no area given, built from two common-height ratios the candidate chooses and a quadrilateral assembled as a sum; (b) two-parameter collinearity with the unknown point on a side produced and no parameter printed - the GCE 2024 P1 Q27(b) technique set without its scaffold, which standard.md section 5 allows once in a paper and this paper does once (the Set's P1 Q27 sets a one-parameter column-vector collinearity, the other paper); (c) the quadrilateral-type justification of GCE 2023 specimen P2 Q6(b)(iii), which no Set has used, reachable only through OE = 3b. One note for the session's read-through: ten marks of pure a-b vector geometry is heavier than the real P2 has placed in one question (the 2023 specimen mixes in column vectors); the slot plan asked for exactly this, so it is recorded, not fixed.

question.stem:
A family is thinking of installing solar panels on the flat roof of their house. They find the following information.

Solar panels
Each panel is a rectangle 1.7 m long and 1.0 m wide, with a rated power of 0.4 kW.
In Singapore, each 1 kW of rated power produces an average of 3.5 kWh of electricity per day.
Cost of panels: $\$650$ per panel, including installation.
Cost of the inverter and wiring: $\$1800$, whatever the number of panels.
Take 1 year to be 365 days.

The roof
The roof is a rectangle 6.4 m by 4.6 m.
The panels are laid flat on the roof with their sides parallel to the edges of the roof, all with their long sides in the same direction and with no gaps between them.
No part of a panel may be within 0.5 m of any edge of the roof.

Electricity
The family buys electricity at 30 cents per kWh.
The family uses 4000 kWh of electricity each year.
Over a year, the family uses the electricity produced by the panels first and buys the rest from the electricity company.
The family is not paid for any electricity produced by the panels that it does not use.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate the amount of electricity, in kWh, that one panel produces in a year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the greatest number of panels that can be installed on the roof.
parts.answer: $10$ panels (long sides parallel to the 4.6 m edge: $5$ across the 5.4 m by $2$ along the 3.6 m; the other way round gives only $3 \times 3 = 9$)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The family wants to install as many panels as possible.
The total cost of the panels, the inverter and the wiring must be paid back within 6 years by the money the family saves on electricity.
Suggest the number of panels the family should install.
Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.answer: $8$ panels: the saving can never exceed $4000 \times \$0.30 = \$1200$ a year, so 10 panels ($\$8300$) take $6.92$ years to pay back and 9 panels ($\$7650$) take $6.38$ years, both too long; 8 panels ($\$7000$, producing $4088$ kWh, which is more than $4000$ kWh) take $5.83$ years, within 6 years. So 8 panels.

question.answer: (a) $511$ kWh; (b) $10$; (c) $8$ panels (payback $5.83$ years; 9 and 10 panels take more than 6 years because electricity beyond the family's $4000$ kWh saves nothing)
skills: greatest number of equal rectangles that fit in a rectangle once a border is removed, trying both orientations and taking whole numbers in each direction (dividing the areas overcounts)

annual saving capped at the household's own use: kWh the family would have bought are worth the buying price, kWh beyond that are worth nothing, so the saving never exceeds 4000 x $0.30 however many panels there are

payback period as (fixed cost + cost per panel x number) divided by the annual saving, searched downward from the roof's maximum to the largest number of panels that pays back within the limit (or the cap on the saving turned into 1800 + 650n <= 6 x 1200)
question.solution:
(a)
One panel produces $0.4 \times 3.5 = 1.4$ kWh per day.
In a year: $1.4 \times 365 = 511$ kWh.
**Answer:** $511$ kWh

(b)
The usable part of the roof is $(6.4 - 2 \times 0.5)$ m by $(4.6 - 2 \times 0.5)$ m $= 5.4$ m by $3.6$ m.
Long sides parallel to the 6.4 m edge: $5.4 \div 1.7 = 3.17$, so 3 panels along; $3.6 \div 1.0 = 3.6$, so 3 panels across. Total $3 \times 3 = 9$.
Long sides parallel to the 4.6 m edge: $3.6 \div 1.7 = 2.12$, so 2 panels along; $5.4 \div 1.0 = 5.4$, so 5 panels across. Total $2 \times 5 = 10$.
**Answer:** $10$ panels

(c)
With $n$ panels the electricity produced in a year is $511n$ kWh.
The family uses $4000$ kWh a year and is not paid for electricity it does not use.
So the most the family can save is $4000 \times \$0.30 = \$1200$ a year.
$8$ panels produce $8 \times 511 = 4088$ kWh, more than $4000$ kWh, so $8$ or more panels all save $\$1200$ a year.
Total cost $= 1800 + 650n$ dollars.

10 panels (the greatest number that fits, from (b)):
Cost $= 1800 + 6500 = \$8300$.
Payback $= 8300 \div 1200 = 6.92$ years, more than 6 years. Not acceptable.

9 panels:
Cost $= 1800 + 5850 = \$7650$.
Payback $= 7650 \div 1200 = 6.38$ years, more than 6 years. Not acceptable.

8 panels:
Cost $= 1800 + 5200 = \$7000$.
Payback $= 7000 \div 1200 = 5.83$ years, within 6 years. Acceptable.

8 is the largest number of panels that fits on the roof and pays back within 6 years.
**Answer:** $8$ panels

(Alternative: in 6 years the saving is at most $6 \times 1200 = \$7200$, so $1800 + 650n \le 7200$, $n \le 8.3$, at most $8$ panels; and $8$ panels produce $4088 \ge 4000$ kWh, so the full saving is made.)

(Note for the marker: a candidate who values all the electricity at 30 cents gets $5110 \times 0.30 = \$1533$ a year for 10 panels and a payback of $5.41$ years, and wrongly chooses 10 panels; the cap at the family's own use is the point of the question.)
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Problems in real-world contexts: reading an information sheet, rates (kWh per day per kW, cents per kWh), money, whole-number fitting of rectangles, a justified decision. No topic outside the syllabus.
question.originality_note: Solar panels on a roof where electricity beyond the family's own use earns nothing. Not a rainwater tank chosen for capacity and footprint (Set 1 P2 Q9), not shuttle buses and a queue (Set 2 P2 Q9), not gym plans (Set 2 P1 Q15); not the candle moulds and packs of GCE 2024 P2 Q9 nor the electric-car charging legs of GCE 2025 P2 Q9. The constraint that changes the answer is the cap on the saving at the family's 4000 kWh: valuing everything at 30 cents gives a believable but wrong 10 panels. There is no second rate, so it does not repeat the two-block tariff of Q2 of this paper. Part (b) is a packing count with an orientation decision (area division gives 11), not a check that one object's footprint fits a base.

answers.(c): 8 panels: 8 panels produce 4088 kWh > 4000 kWh, so saving = 4000 x $0.30 = $1200 a year, $7200 in 6 years >= cost 8 x 650 + 1800 = $7000 (pays back); 9 panels cost $7650 > $7200 (does not); 7 panels: 6-yr saving $6438.60 >= $6350 also pays back but 8 is more

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give 511 kWh. Checked: 0.4 x 3.5 = 1.4 kWh a day, x 365 = 511.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 10 panels. Checked: usable area (6.4 - 1.0) by (4.6 - 1.0) = 5.4 m by 3.6 m; long sides along the 3.6 m side gives floor(3.6/1.7) = 2 by floor(5.4/1.0) = 5 = 10; the other way floor(5.4/1.7) = 3 by 3 = 9; dividing the areas, 19.44/1.7 = 11.4, overcounts to 11. All wrong routes land on tidy numbers (9 or 11).

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both give 8 panels by the same inequality, the setter as payback years and the examiner as six years' saving against cost. Checked: saving = 0.30 x min(511n, 4000) a year, so never more than 1200; 10 panels cost 8300 (6.92 years), 9 cost 7650 (6.38 years), both fail; 8 cost 7000 and produce 4088 >= 4000 kWh, 5.83 years, passes; 7 also passes (6350 against 6 x 1073.10 = 6438.60) but is fewer. The alternative 1800 + 650n <= 7200 gives n <= 8.3, with the 4088 >= 4000 check closing it. Valuing every kWh at 30 cents gives 10 panels at 5.41 years, the intended wrong answer.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on every part and the key is right; I reworked all three parts.
fixes: Say that the panels are laid with their sides parallel to the edges of the roof ("laid flat on the roof with their sides parallel to the edges of the roof, all with their long sides in the same direction and with no gaps between them"); as printed, a tilted arrangement is not excluded, and a real paper closes that door.
Register: "Take 1 year $= 365$ days." -> "Take 1 year to be 365 days." (SEAB does not print an equals sign inside a sentence of the stem).
verdict.why: A real last question in the 2024/25 shape (a 1-mark opener, a 3-mark packing decision with a border and both orientations, then a 6-mark justify needing item 10's two explicit decisions: that electricity beyond the family's own 4000 kWh saves nothing, and a search down from the roof's 10 to the largest number that pays back within 6 years), with a believable wrong answer (10 panels at 5.41 years) and clean numbers; the deciding parts carry 9 of 10 marks. Not a re-skin of GCE 2024 P2 Q9 (candle pricing) or GCE 2025 P2 Q9 (charging times and cost); its skills (packing with a border, a saving capped at own use, a payback search) are new to the Sets (Set 1 P2 Q9 chose a tank, Set 2 P2 Q9 sized a bus fleet), and the earlier defect, an 8-cent sell-back that made a two-block rate echoing this paper's Q2, has been removed (the family is now simply not paid for surplus), so no skill or closing step is reused in the paper. Beside Set 1 P2 Q9 the (c) constraint changes the answer the same way (the cap rejects 9 and 10 as the base rejects the preferred tank) and (b) is a stronger 3-mark decision than Set 1's rainfall back-calculation. Gates all pass. Two wording edits keep it at 4.
